The Common wallaroo (Macropus robustus) exhibits a suite of life-history traits typical of large-bodied macropodids inhabiting semi-arid and rocky environments across Australia. Neonates are remarkably altricial at birth, with newborns weighing just 0.703 grams [Wwb = 0.703 grams], a mass that reflects the species' reliance on a prolonged period of post-natal development within the maternal pouch. This extremely small size at parturition, characteristic of marsupials, necessitates an extended period of lactation and maternal investment before the young can achieve nutritional independence. The suckling juvenile undergoes a steady growth trajectory while receiving milk from the female, and weaning — marking the end of maternal provisioning — occurs when the young wallaroo reaches a wet weight of approximately 2500 grams [Wwx = approximately 2500 grams]. This threshold represents a critical transition point in the offspring's life, as it must then rely entirely on foraging to cover its ongoing energy requirements.

At the species' typical core body temperature of 36.1 °C [T = 36.1 °C], females produce a single offspring per litter [N_R_i = single offspring per litter], and maximum reproduction rates indicate that they can sustain approximately 1.4 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 1.4 litters per year]. This characteristically low rate reflects the substantial period between successive births, as females must complete the gestation of the new embryo — which lasts 32 days [tg = 32 days] — and subsequently carry the developing pouch young through an extended period of dependency at a temperature of 36.1 °C [T = 36.1 °C]. The combination of singleton births and this prolonged interval between reproductive events strongly limits the species' maximum annual productivity, a pattern consistent with other large herbivores exhibiting K-selected life-history strategies.

The developmental schedule of Macropus robustus unfolds over a long temporal scale, particularly when compared to smaller eutherian mammals of similar body size. Young wallaroos achieve nutritional independence at weaning, which occurs at 351 days since birth [tx = 351 days since birth] when maintained at a stable core temperature of 36.1 °C [T = 36.1 °C]. This extended period of lactation and pouch residence is typical of macropodids and serves to protect the altricial neonate while allowing its demanding somatic growth to proceed within a safe environment. Following weaning, juveniles enter a sub-adult phase during which they continue to grow in size and accumulate body reserves before reaching sexual maturity. The time since birth at the onset of puberty for females is 547 days since birth [tp = 547 days since birth], while males require a considerably longer developmental period to achieve gonadal maturation, reaching puberty at 670 days since birth [tp = 670 days since birth] under identical thermal conditions at a temperature of 36.1 °C [T = 36.1 °C] at a temperature of 36.1 °C [T = 36.1 °C]. This pronounced sexual dimorphism in the timing of maturation likely reflects the different selective pressures operating on male and female reproductive strategies in this species.

Maximum body size in the Common wallaroo is substantial, with individuals attaining a very large adult stature typical of the genus Macropus. The ultimate wet weight, or maximum recorded body mass in adults, is 30000 grams [Wwi = 30000 grams], a value observed in prime-condition individuals inhabiting productive lowland habitats with abundant forage. This considerable mass places M. robustus among the larger extant macropodids and is associated with a correspondingly low instantaneous mortality rate and extended lifespan. Under field conditions at their typical core body temperature of 36.1 °C [T = 36.1 °C], the maximum recorded longevity for wild individuals is 8030 days [am = 8030 days], a duration that is remarkably long for an Australian marsupial herbivore and reflects the species' relatively slow life-history pace and low adult predation pressure in its preferred rocky refuges. Such a lengthy lifespan provides extensive opportunities for repeated reproductive events across an individual's lifetime.

Gestation, at 32 days [tg = 32 days], is relatively short compared to the total period of offspring dependency, a trait that allows females to maintain a continuous reproductive capacity through embryonic diapause — a strategy in which a new blastocyst remains quiescent in the uterus until the current pouch young vacates the teat at a temperature of 36.1 °C [T = 36.1 °C]. Following parturition, the altricial newborn weighing just 0.703 grams [Wwb = 0.703 grams] begins its progressive development inside the pouch, with weaning occurring at 351 days since birth [tx = 351 days since birth] at 36.1 °C [T = 36.1 °C]. After nutritional independence, female juveniles attain puberty at 547 days since birth [tp = 547 days since birth] at 36.1 °C [T = 36.1 °C], a full 119 days earlier than their male counterparts, which require 670 days since birth [tp = 670 days since birth] at 36.1 °C [T = 36.1 °C] to complete testicular descent and gametogenesis. Over a maximum lifespan of 8030 days [am = 8030 days] at 36.1 °C [T = 36.1 °C], an individual female can therefore invest in multiple litters, each containing a single offspring [N_R_i = each containing a single offspring], and ultimately achieve an adult body mass up to 30000 grams [Wwi = up to 30000 grams], underscoring the species' profoundly K-selected demographic strategy.
